clue.text: After a moment, artist kills old beast

indicators.note: the artist comes after the moment, so this word fixes the order of the first two pieces

parts.note: a trice is a very short moment
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist
to top someone is slang for to kill them, so tops means kills

explanation.surface: An artist pauses briefly and then finishes off an ancient animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kills' looks like the main verb but supplies TOPS, a slangy sense of 'kills'.
explanation.definitionFit: This horned, three-horned dinosaur died out millions of years ago, an extinct prehistoric creature.

clue.text: True right takes ale when drunk

indicators.note: drunk suggests something scrambled and unsteady, so the word ale is rearranged

explanation.surface: A man who is truly in the right still reaches for a beer once drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' reads as describing the drinker, but 'when drunk' is the anagram signal for the beer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something genuine or actual is true, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: It can be rotten, having to go to bed

definitions.text: It can be rotten, having to go to bed

parts.words: It can be rotten, having to go to bed
parts.note: reads like a grumble about bedtime, but describes decayed garden matter that gardeners spread on flower beds

explanation.surface: Being sent off to bed early can feel rotten.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bed' is a garden bed, and 'rotten' is literal: decomposed vegetable matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotted plant waste is dug into garden beds as fertiliser, so it is literally rotten and goes to bed.

clue.text: Indian music when the jelly's served up

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the word is brought upwards, read from bottom to top

parts.note: agar is a jelly made from seaweed; the 's here stands for is and gives no letter

explanation.surface: A dessert of jelly comes out to the sound of Indian music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' reverses AGAR to give RAGA in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional melodic framework of Indian classical music, used as the basis for improvisation.

clue.text: Work with us to entertain king and Trojan prince

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to hold them within, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: toil is hard work
R is short for rex, Latin for king
us taken as written, attached to the rest

explanation.surface: A labour shared with others is laid on for a monarch and a prince of Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entertain' sounds like amusing a king, but here it means taking him in as a guest, the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A son of King Priam of Troy, hero of Chaucer's and Shakespeare's love stories with Cressida.

clue.text: Suffering is obvious when liberal is ousted

indicators.note: ousted means thrown out, so the letter for liberal is removed from the word

parts.note: plain means clear or obvious

explanation.surface: Distress is plain to see when a Liberal politician is thrown out of office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is ousted' removes the L from PLAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurt or agony is a form of suffering, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Pipe-smokers kept outside the house

parts.note: suggests people banished outdoors to smoke, but describes the clay pipes on a roof through which household smoke escapes

explanation.surface: Pipe smokers are made to stand outside the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'pipes' are flues on the roof, which give off smoke from the fires inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The terracotta pipes atop a roof's stack carry smoke away from the fireplaces below.

clue.text: Gal bursting with bonhomie — it's in the blood

indicators.note: bursting suggests breaking apart, so the letters of gal and bonhomie are rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl is overflowing with good cheer, a cheerfulness that runs in her blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bursting' shuffles GAL plus BONHOMIE, eleven letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: The iron-rich protein carrying oxygen in red cells is found in the bloodstream.

clue.text: Murderous types moving with a tender hush

indicators.note: moving suggests the letters are shifted about, so a tender hush is rearranged

explanation.surface: Killers creep forward in a gentle silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges the eleven letters of A TENDER HUSH.
explanation.definitionFit: Tribesmen who took enemies' skulls as trophies were killers by custom.

clue.text: Being indomitable, I deserve any break

indicators.note: break suggests smashing the words apart, so I deserve any is rearranged

explanation.surface: An unbeatable person claims to have earned every rest they get.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' rearranges the letters of I DESERVE ANY.
explanation.definitionFit: A refusal to give up, a stubborn never-quit spirit, is what indomitable describes.

clue.text: Oppressed, being under 11?

definitions.meaning: kept down and treated harshly by those in power
11-across is a body part at the back of the foot, so being beneath it means being crushed underfoot

explanation.walkthrough: The 11 refers to 11-across; to be under someone's heel is to be trodden down.
explanation.definitionFit: Crushed beneath a heel is trampled, and tyrannised people are said to be trampled.

clue.text: Part of body to get better, we've heard

indicators.note: something we have heard is spoken, so the word for getting better is replaced by one that sounds the same

parts.note: to heal is to recover or get better

explanation.surface: A part of the body needs time to recover, so we are told.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for 'get better' sounds just like the back of the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The rounded back of the foot is a body part.

clue.text: Captain given ominous sign heading west

indicators.note: in an across clue, heading west means reading right to left

parts.note: an omen is a sign, often of something bad

explanation.surface: A sea captain sees a foreboding sign as the ship sails west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading west' reverses OMEN. Captain Nemo commands the submarine Nautilus in Jules Verne's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Verne's submarine commander bears this captain's name.

clue.text: Stop going the wrong way in crowd — it's lunacy

indicators.note: in places the reversed piece inside the word for crowd

parts.note: a mass is a large crowd

indicators.note: going the wrong way means the word for stop is read backwards

parts.note: end means stop or finish

explanation.surface: Walking against the flow in a throng is plain insanity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop' looks like an order, but it is a noun for the finish, turned round by 'going the wrong way' and set 'in' the crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Insanity or folly is madness, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Sarah, operating in beauty parlour?

parts.note: Sal is a short form of Sarah
on means working or operating, as in a machine switched on

explanation.surface: Sarah is at work in a beauty parlour.
explanation.walkthrough: SAL is a pet form of Sarah; the question mark admits the definition is just one kind of salon.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairdressing or beauty businesses are commonly called salons, a shop sense of the word.

clue.text: Plant a German found on Scottish island

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece found on another sits after it

parts.note: Mull is an island in the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland
ein is German for a

explanation.surface: A plant belonging to a German turns up on a Scottish isle.
explanation.walkthrough: MULL is a Scottish island in the Inner Hebrides; EIN is the German for 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall woolly-leaved herb with yellow flower spikes, a wild flowering plant.

clue.text: Saying as much as possible without hesitation ultimately

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the hesitation sound is dropped from the longer word
ultimately says the dropped letters come off the very end of the word

parts.note: the maximum is the most possible
um is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: An adage tells us to give our utmost without dithering in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' and 'ultimately' remove UM from the end of MAXIMUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A short pithy saying or principle, such as a proverb or adage.

clue.text: Dad sat around outside — snack served

indicators.note: outside means the reversed word goes round the word for father
around means the word sat is turned back to front

parts.note: Pa is an informal word for dad

explanation.surface: Father lounged outdoors while nibbles were brought out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' reverses the word sat; 'outside' then wraps those letters round the father. The plural answer stands for a singular 'snack'.
explanation.definitionFit: Small Spanish savoury dishes served with drinks are eaten as a light bite. The answer is plural against a singular definition, a common looseness.

clue.text: Birds featured in the musical

indicators.note: featured in says the answer appears within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Some birds have a role in the stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'featured in' tells you the answer sits inside 'the musical'.
explanation.definitionFit: Large flightless Australian runners are birds.

clue.text: America's first lady as an employer

parts.note: US is short for the United States of America
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the queen, first lady of the land

explanation.surface: The President's wife is cast as the one who hires staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first lady' suggests the US President's wife, but it is ER, the Queen (Elizabeth Regina).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who employs a thing makes use of it, so an employer in this sense is one who uses.

clue.text: Design test in connection with poem

parts.note: MOT is the annual British roadworthiness test for vehicles
If is a famous poem by Rudyard Kipling

explanation.surface: A pattern is tried out in connection with a piece of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The MOT is Britain's yearly roadworthiness check for cars; 'If' is Kipling's famous poem.
explanation.definitionFit: A recurring decorative pattern or theme is a motif.

clue.text: Maureen gets to flog English or German wine

parts.note: Mo is a short form of Maureen
to flog is slang for to sell

explanation.surface: Maureen gets to market English or German wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flog' means to beat, but in British slang it means to sell.
explanation.definitionFit: A white wine from the valley of the river of that name in Germany.

clue.text: Sweet little boy placed in vessel for baptism

indicators.note: placed in means one piece is set inside the other

parts.note: a font is the basin used for baptism in a church
Dan is a short form of Daniel, a boy's name

explanation.surface: A small child is set in the font at a christening, with a sweet afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' suggests a ship, but it is the church basin; 'placed in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft sugar paste used for icing and confectionery is a kind of sweet.

clue.text: Exploited don goes around university quietly

indicators.note: goes around means the phrase for don wraps round the other pieces

parts.note: to don clothes is to put them on
p, piano, is the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: A university lecturer quietly does the rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'don' looks like a university lecturer but is the verb meaning to dress in; 'goes around' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone taken advantage of is exploited, a set phrase for being imposed on.

clue.text: Well-off managing director, one you embraced

indicators.note: embraced means the first piece hugs the others inside it

parts.note: one taken as written
ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: A wealthy company boss is the one you hugged.
explanation.walkthrough: YE is the old form of 'you'; 'embraced' is the container signal around the director's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Being rich, having plenty of cash, is being well-off.

clue.text: Audibly rip old weed

indicators.note: audibly means we hear the word for rip, and write a word with the same sound

parts.note: to tear is to rip

explanation.surface: Noisily pull up an ancient weed.
explanation.walkthrough: The rip word sounds like a weed named in the Bible's parable of the wheat.
explanation.definitionFit: A biblical name for weeds sown among wheat, usually taken as darnel or vetch.

clue.text: One boy from among the millions

indicators.note: from among says the answer is taken out of the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A single lad is picked out from the masses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from among' says the answer sits inside 'the millions'.
explanation.definitionFit: A male first name, as in the children's book hero of Emil and the Detectives.

clue.text: Acoustic property of city house

parts.note: EC is the postal district covering the City of London

explanation.surface: A town hall's sound qualities are being described.
explanation.walkthrough: EC is the postcode area for the City, London's financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: Reflected sound bouncing back off surfaces is a feature of a room's acoustics.

clue.text: I had to be carried by aged assistant

indicators.note: carried by means held within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: ae, short for Latin aetatis, means aged
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: An old helper is left to carry someone.
explanation.walkthrough: AE abbreviates Latin aetatis, 'aged', as on old portraits and tombstones. 'to be carried by' puts ID inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A helper or aide-de-camp is an assistant.

clue.text: Illness that's unclear getting five wiped out

indicators.note: wiped out means the Roman numeral for five is erased

parts.note: vague means unclear
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: A mysterious sickness has wiped out five people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wiped out' looks like a killing, but it drops V from VAGUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A fever with shivering fits, typically malaria, is an illness.

clue.text: A bit of money needed to make minor adjustment

definitions.meaning: coins of low value carried loose in a pocket

explanation.surface: Only a little cash is needed to make a small tweak.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose coins are a few pence; a slight alteration is a modest shift, the same phrase in both senses.

clue.text: Coppers showing courage when overrun by Oxbridge types

indicators.note: overrun by means the courage word is surrounded by the other

parts.note: blues are sportspeople who have represented Oxford or Cambridge
bottle is British slang for nerve or courage

explanation.surface: Police officers show their nerve when swamped by Oxford and Cambridge students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' could be coins, but it is police. A blue is an Oxford or Cambridge sporting award; bluebottle is old slang for a policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang for policemen, from their blue uniforms.
